title: Strict log-concavity in the first type-B q-Stirling column
summary: In the first column of the second-kind array, strict log-concavity begins at row six.
verification: The classification was formally checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: The exact threshold at rank six identifies where the proposed strict inequality begins to hold throughout the first column.
what_this_settles: In the first column of the type-B Stirling numbers of the second kind, every interior coefficient satisfies strict log-concavity exactly from rank six onward.

title: A 19-vertex counterexample to Graffiti.pc 138
summary: A tree whose longest path has 17 vertices, one fewer than the conjecture requires.
verification: Direct proof and an exhaustive check of the 19-vertex tree.
why_it_matters: The tree explains how the proposed path bound fails, and extending its spine makes the shortfall arbitrarily large.
what_this_settles: A 19-vertex tree has a longest induced path of 17 vertices where Graffiti.pc Conjecture 138 requires at least 18, disproving the conjecture.

title: Graffiti.pc 392b on 2-domination and matchings
summary: A matching bound on the number of vertices needed to give every unmarked vertex two marked neighbors.
verification: The full theorem was formally checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: The matching bound gives a guarantee for every connected graph with at least three vertices, including graphs with leaves.
what_this_settles: The matching bound in Graffiti.pc Conjecture 392b holds for every finite simple connected graph with at least three vertices.

title: One-sided log-concavity for a column of the type B q-Stirling numbers
summary: Proves the parity inequality on the rising side of first-kind column one at every rank, and on the second diagonal of both families. The unrestricted conjecture remains open.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: The result locates a whole range of coefficients where the conjectured inequality holds across ranks, even though the unrestricted case remains open.
what_this_settles: The parity log-concavity inequality holds on the rising side of first-kind column one and on the second diagonal of both type-B families, leaving the other cases open.

title: Coefficient inequalities for the type B q-Stirling numbers
summary: A combined technical note on seven Lean-verified results. Strict adjacent log-concavity in second-kind column one begins at rank six for ranks at least two. The note also proves a rising-side inequality in first-kind column one and parity log-concavity on the second diagonal of both families.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: The combined treatment shows which coefficient inequalities are known across the two families and where the general conjecture remains open.
what_this_settles: The combined results establish the rank-six threshold for strict log-concavity in second-kind column one and prove special cases of the parity inequalities in Sagan–Swanson Conjecture 7.5.

title: Two partial results on the Seacrest–Seacrest graph-grabbing conjecture
summary: On even connected bipartite graphs with no induced once-subdivided claw, Alice can secure half the weight if adjacent positive weights agree. A second result compares opposite choices of the last vertex on a path with attached leaves. The general conjecture remains open.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: The weight condition identifies a class of bipartite boards on which Alice can guarantee half the total weight.
what_this_settles: Alice can guarantee half the total weight on even connected bipartite graphs with no induced once-subdivided claw when adjacent positive weights agree.

title: A counterexample to Songsuwan’s period-two conjecture for Node-Kayles
summary: On a fixed 291-vertex graph, attach copies of the same five-vertex path at one vertex. The Node-Kayles values are 8 and 9 at arbitrarily large branch counts two apart. This disproves Songsuwan’s Conjecture 2.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: Even after arbitrarily many identical branches are attached, adding two more can still change the game value, overturning the proposed long-run pattern.
what_this_settles: Adding two identical branches can change the Node-Kayles value even at arbitrarily large branch counts, disproving Songsuwan’s Conjecture 2.

title: A uniform lower bound on the transient length of the consecutive-231 stack map
summary: For every n ≥ 8, some permutation of length n takes at least n + 3 passes of the consecutive-231 stack map to reach a periodic point.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: A construction for every length from eight onward raises the known lower bound on how many passes this sorting rule can take.
what_this_settles: For every length n ≥ 8, some permutation takes at least n + 3 passes of the consecutive-231 stack map to reach a periodic point, leaving the maximum delay open.

title: Armstrong’s Catalan ribbon partition conjecture at a = 6
summary: At a = 6, all nine slices of the fundamental box admit partitions into six-point saturated chains. The 1,296 ribbons cover all 7,776 points.
verification: The formal proof was checked in Lean.
why_it_matters: Explicit chains cover all nine slices for the six-ribbon case, giving a complete construction that can be checked point by point.
what_this_settles: All nine slices admit the required ribbon partition at a = 6, proving that case of Armstrong’s conjecture.

title: A positional proof for a 19-letter subsequence cover
summary: Only the full word can cover every position of abacadbabdcabcbadac by subsequence occurrences.
verification: Pinned Lean replay of WordSPrimitivityReplay.exact_claim and an independent exact computation.
explainer: Pick one shorter word and try to cover every letter of abacadbabdcabcbadac with occurrences of it. Each occurrence may skip letters, and different occurrences may cover different positions. The three copies of d force an unexpectedly rigid choice: a covering word must use all three. That pins its four intervening and end pieces in place and forces the entire original word. This answers the authors’ request for a computer-free proof for this particular word.
why_it_matters: The authors knew the answer by computation, and the positions of the three d’s explain by hand why every shorter word fails.
what_this_settles: Only the full 19-letter word abacadbabdcabcbadac can cover all its positions by subsequence occurrences, answering the authors’ request for a computer-free proof.

title: One-edge closures with consecutive breaks in log-concavity
summary: Three explicit one-edge closures answer Levit and Kadrawi’s Problem 6.6 for both named tree constructions.
verification: Pinned Lean replay of UnicyclicClosure.problem_6_6 and an independent exact computation.
explainer: Count the ways to pick k vertices of a graph with no edges between them. As k grows, those counts can go up to a single peak and then drop, yet still bend the wrong way compared with their neighbors. Can several such bends survive after one extra edge closes a tree into a cycle? Three explicit graphs show that they can. The 315-vertex example has three consecutive breaks and still has a single peak. This settles the existence question; minimal graph sizes remain open.
why_it_matters: Explicit examples from both named tree constructions answer the existence question, including a graph with three consecutive failures of log-concavity.
what_this_settles: Both tree constructions in Levit and Kadrawi’s Problem 6.6 admit a one-edge closure with consecutive failures of log-concavity.

title: A sublogarithmic bound for integral arctangent-sum values
summary: Through N, the number of indices n ≥ 5 at which the arctangent-sum tangent is an integer is O((log N)^(3/4)).
verification: Lean checks the asymptotic bound for the literal Gaussian divisibility predicate.
explainer: Add the angles whose tangents are the integers from 1 to n, then take the tangent of the sum. Can the answer be an integer once n reaches five? Amdeberhan, Medina and Moll conjectured that it never is. This result limits how often an exception could occur. Among the first N indices, the count grows at most like the three-quarters power of the logarithm of N. The estimate still allows isolated exceptions.
why_it_matters: The new bound improves the logarithmic estimate for how often an integer value could occur, while leaving open whether any occur after the first four terms.
what_this_settles: Among indices from 5 through N, at most O((log N)^(3/4)) yield an integer tangent, leaving open whether any such index exists.

title: Least periods of Moll’s signed arctangent companion sequence
summary: Gives the least eventual period of Moll’s signed real sequence modulo every positive integer and characterizes periods from index zero.
verification: Four proof modules rebuilt with pinned Lean and standard axioms. An independent prime-power review and finite state checks on 168 moduli agree.
explainer:
Victor Moll studied the real part of the running product $(1+i)(1+2i)\cdots(1+ni)$ with an alternating sign. His paper gives several periods modulo primes and proposes a formula based on the prime’s residue modulo eight. The exact period depends on the multiplicative order of $-2$ instead. For example, modulo 31 that order is 10, and the least period is 310 rather than the 930 proposed by the residue-class formula.

The proof compares a handful of terms near the initial index with the same terms one period later. For odd moduli, these comparisons recover the index modulo the modulus and both coordinates of the running Gaussian product. A full block then acts by a scalar. The result gives the least eventual period modulo every positive integer, and determines exactly when the pattern repeats from the start. The conjecture that the original tangent sums are nonintegral for every $n\ge5$ remains open.
why_it_matters: The period modulo 31 overturns the proposed formula, and the replacement theorem gives the least eventual period for every positive modulus.
what_this_settles: The result determines the least eventual period for every positive modulus and disproves Moll’s proposed prime-modulus formula at 31.

title: Equal-length ribbons in Armstrong’s sum-two slice
summary: Partitions the sum-two slice into saturated chains of the prescribed length for every odd parameter and gives the reflected slice by complementation.
verification: Pinned Lean proof for the sum-two cut with standard axioms. Separate mathematical review checks the exact source statement and the written reflection.
what_this_settles: Armstrong’s Conjecture 10.2 holds at the cut $c=2$ and the reflected cut $c=(a-1)^2-2$ for every odd $a\ge3$, with the first cut checked in Lean and the reflected cut deduced in writing, while the general all-cut conjecture remains open.
explainer: Drew Armstrong asks whether lattice points between successive coprime cuts can be partitioned into chains that visit one point at each successive rank and contain exactly $a$ points. At the cut where the coordinates sum to two, each point gives two occupied positions, with repetition allowed. Order those positions as a pair. Each chain starts by increasing the longer column and then alternates column increases. For example, when $a=7$ one seven-point chain runs from $(0,0)$ along $(0,j)$ through $(0,5)$ and then to $(1,5)$. The construction works at this cut for every odd $a\ge3$. Complementing the coordinates gives the reflected single slice. The general conjecture over all cuts remains open. [Armstrong’s paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00026-026-00819-9)
why_it_matters: A single geometric rule extends Armstrong’s small-parameter sum-two examples to every odd parameter and also gives their reflected partitions.

title: A sharp real-root range for Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators
summary: Determines the sharp nonnegative parameter interval for simultaneous real-rootedness of all second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators and checks two subsidiary assertions in Lin and Zeng.
verification: Written proof · independent AI mathematical review
what_this_settles: For every nonnegative real parameter \(u\), all second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators of index \(k\ge1\) are real-rooted exactly when \(u\le\rho\), with the second diagonal already having nonreal zeros above \(\rho\) and the negative-parameter classification outside the scope of this proof.
explainer:
The Jacobi–Stirling numbers form a triangular array controlled by a parameter \(u\). Each fixed diagonal has a generating series with a polynomial numerator. Lin and Zeng studied when the zeros are all nonpositive. Here the question is when every numerator has real zeros, allowing either sign.

The first diagonal already has a positive zero when \(u>1\). At \(u=2\) the second numerator still has only real zeros. As the parameter increases beyond \(2\), two positive zeros meet at \(\rho\) and then become a nonreal pair. The second diagonal determines the exact threshold. Below and at that threshold, a weighted derivative argument accounts for every zero on the two real intervals outside \([0,1]\) at each later step.

For nonnegative \(u\), the range is the closed interval from zero to the threshold \(\rho\), which lies between \(41/20\) and \(33/16\). The proof also supplies the exact degree at every real parameter and an example where a diagonal numerator has no positive zero despite \(u>1\).
why_it_matters: This extends the known range for real zeros beyond the nonpositive-root range of Lin and Zeng and shows that checking the first two diagonals completely decides the all-diagonal question for nonnegative parameters.

title: The sharp negative parameter range for Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators
summary: Determines the sharp negative parameter range for simultaneous real-rootedness of all second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators and gives the root locations and endpoint multiplicities.
verification: Written proof · independent AI mathematical review
what_this_settles: For every real \(u<0\), all second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators of index \(k\ge1\) are real-rooted exactly when \(u\ge-1-\sigma\), including the endpoint where \(\sigma\) is the unique nonnegative zero of the polynomial in the proof.
explainer:
The second-kind Jacobi–Stirling numbers form a triangular array that depends on a real parameter \(u\). Each diagonal has a generating function whose numerator is a polynomial. The question is how far below zero \(u\) can go while every one of those polynomials still has only real zeros.

At \(u=-6/5\), all the diagonal numerators have real zeros. Apart from the factor \(x\), the second numerator has three negative zeros, one in each of the intervals cut out by \(-2,-1,-1/20,0\). The odd diagonals each have one positive zero. The proof uses the first three generating-series coefficients to control where two negative zeros appear at each odd-to-even step.

There is an exact cutoff between \(-121/100\) and \(-6/5\). The cutoff is included, even though two roots of the second numerator coincide there. At every more negative parameter the second numerator has a nonreal pair.
why_it_matters: The result extends Lin and Zeng's nonpositive-root range to the exact negative cutoff for real zeros and shows that the second diagonal decides the question for the whole family.

title: A certificate for three full layers in the seven-cube
summary: Every subset of the seven-cube with no three distinct points on a real line and a 14-point layer perpendicular to each coordinate axis has at most 86 points.
verification: Computer-assisted proof · independent AI mathematical review
what_this_settles: Every subset of the seven-cube with no three distinct real-collinear points and a 14-point layer perpendicular to each of the three coordinate axes has at most 86 points, and the unrestricted maximum remains open.
explainer:
How many points can a seven-by-seven-by-seven grid hold if no three distinct points lie on a straight line? A coordinate layer can hold at most 14 points, because its seven rows can hold at most two apiece. We check whether 87 points can fit when each coordinate direction has a layer of 14.

Once three full layers are fixed, any site on a line through two of their points is ruled out. Counting the sites that can still fit in each of the other layers usually gives an upper bound below 87. In the remaining cases the checker lists every possible pattern for one additional layer and closes each branch. For example, one triple of full layers at height zero leaves a single 13-point pattern in the layer at $z=3$ if the total is to reach 87. Fixing that pattern reduces the bound to 78 by counting along parallel lines.

The complete replay shows that a set with three full perpendicular layers has at most 86 points. The exact maximum without the layer condition remains open. [Original seven-cube problem](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.25133v1#S3)
why_it_matters: The bound adds to the known one-axis layer exclusions by showing that 87 points are impossible with three full perpendicular layers at any heights.

title: A sharp real-root range for Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators
summary: Formalizes the sharp nonnegative cutoff for simultaneous real-rootedness of all positive-rank second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators.
verification: Lean-verified proof · independent AI source review and pinned replay
what_this_settles: For every real parameter (ugeq0), Lean proves that all positive-rank second-kind Jacobi–Stirling diagonal numerators split over the reals exactly when (uleq ho), where (41/20< ho<33/16), with the negative parameters and the two subsidiary assertions covered separately in writing.
explainer: The Jacobi–Stirling numbers form a triangular array controlled by a real parameter. Each diagonal gives a generating series with a polynomial numerator. Lin and Zeng established when these numerators have only nonpositive zeros. Allowing positive zeros gives a wider range. At parameter 2 the second numerator is (x(9+34x-3x^2)), which has three real zeros. As the parameter increases past the cutoff, the second numerator develops a nonreal pair. Up to the cutoff, a change of variable and a weighted polynomial recurrence propagate real splitting to every higher diagonal.
why_it_matters: The sharp cutoff extends Lin and Zeng’s nonpositive-root range and shows that the second diagonal decides whether all the numerators have real zeros for a fixed nonnegative parameter.

title: A four-deletion obstruction for Jacobi–Stirling descent polynomials
summary: At rank 31, strictly positive integer weights on every four-deletion set give a Jacobi–Stirling descent polynomial with nonreal zeros. The all-rank equal-weight case remains open.
verification: Computer-assisted proof · independent AI mathematical review
what_this_settles: At rank 31 and four barred deletions, a strictly positive integer weighting of all 31,465 deletion sets gives a Jacobi–Stirling descent polynomial with nonreal zeros, while Gessel–Lin–Zeng's all-rank equal-weight claim for four deletions remains open.
explainer:
Start with two copies of every label and one barred copy of every label. After deleting four barred copies, count the allowed arrangements by descents, which are places where a letter is followed by a smaller one. This gives one polynomial for each deletion set. Gessel, Lin and Zeng ask whether the equal-weight sum always has real zeros. Ma and Wang proved that every nonnegative weighted sum works for several deletion counts, including one, two and three.

At rank 31, give extra weight to deleting the first four barred labels and to deleting the last four. Every deletion set still receives positive weight, but the resulting polynomial violates an inequality that every polynomial with only real zeros must satisfy. This example rules out a guarantee for all positive weights at four deletions. The all-rank claim for equal weights remains open. [Original conjecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1201.0622) · [Ma–Wang, §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.03111v1#S4)
why_it_matters: Ma and Wang's theorem for arbitrary weights at one, two and three deletions cannot extend to the next deletion count.
